title: Nyaya (logic)
hook: a gray column rises behind the next hill, nobody can see a flame, and everybody says fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nyaya opened with four means of knowing: perception, inference, comparison, and the word of someone reliable. Today, one of the four, up close.
screen: `NYAYA: FOUR MEANS OF KNOWING.` · `ONE OF THEM, UP CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Three friends walk a ridge in the late afternoon. Across the valley, from behind the next hill, a gray column is rising, leaning with the wind. Nobody can see a flame; the hill is in the way. Yet all three say the same word at once: fire. Nobody stops to wonder how they knew a thing none of them can see. Nyaya stops right there. That quick leap is one of its four means of knowing, and the hill with smoke on it is the example its teachers reach for.
screen: `A GRAY COLUMN, NO FLAME.` → `ALL THREE SAY FIRE.` → `HOW DID THEY KNOW?`

segments.voice: The word is anumana: inference, knowing something you can't see by way of a sign you can. Nyaya teachers lay it out in plain pieces. The hill has fire, because it has smoke. What makes that work: smoke and fire have been seen together before, at the kitchen hearth, again and again. The opposite has been seen too: a still lake, no fire, no smoke. From cases like those comes a rule: wherever there's smoke, there's fire. Later Nyaya teachers named that rule vyapti, pervasion: smoke is always found inside the territory of fire. With the rule in hand, the leap isn't a guess. It's knowing. But Nyaya cares just as much how the leap goes wrong. The Nyaya Sutra names reasons that only look like reasons, and teachers give homely examples. One trap: the sign isn't what you think. That gray column might be mist off the trees, or dust from a road. Before you reason from smoke, make sure it's smoke. A second trap: the rule run backward. Wherever there's fire, there's smoke? A red-hot iron ball glows with fire and gives off no smoke. The rule runs one way. These traps turn up everywhere. A closed office door, so the boss is angry. A short reply, so they don't care. Maybe. Or maybe it's mist. Nyaya doesn't ask you to stop inferring; you couldn't live a day without it. It asks two questions first: is the sign real, and does the rule really run this way?
screen: `ANUMANA: FROM A SIGN TO THE UNSEEN.` · `SMOKE AND FIRE AT THE HEARTH.` · `IS IT SMOKE, OR MIST?` · `THE RULE RUNS ONE WAY.` · then, large: `IS THE SIGN REAL?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a conclusion you reached this week about someone from a sign, a look, a silence, a tone of voice, and ask: was it really what I took it for, or could it have been mist? Then ask whether you know this sign always comes with that meaning. Don't decide anything; just let the leap slow down until you can see it, and if you pray, ask the God you know for clear eyes.
Nyaya. Today, anumana, inference: the hill has fire because it has smoke, as long as it's really smoke, and the rule really runs that way.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Is it smoke, or is it mist? See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit study, students of Nyaya learn inference through the example of smoke and fire on a hill, practicing how to state a sign, a rule and a supporting case, and how to spot reasons that only look like reasons.

notes: Second Nyaya day. Takes inference (smoke and fire), which day 1162 deliberately left aside; 1162's review asks where the listener jumped to a conclusion, which this carry sets up.

The smoke-fire example, the hearth (mahanasa) and lake (hrada) cases, mist or dust mistaken for smoke, and the red-hot iron ball (ayogolaka) are from the later Nyaya teaching tradition (e.g. Tarkasangraha), not the Sutra's own words; attributed to 'Nyaya teachers'. Confirm.
'Vyapti' is attributed to 'later Nyaya teachers'; confirm it is fair not to place it in the Sutra.
